stages.title: René Descartes and rationalism
stages.hook: Suppose every belief you hold might be false. Is there anything you could not doubt? Try to find one before reading on.
explain: René Descartes (1596 to 1650), a French thinker who lived much of his life in the Dutch Republic, wanted knowledge that could not be shaken. In his Meditations (1641) he adopted a method of doubt: reject anything that can be doubted and see what remains. Senses sometimes deceive us, we may be dreaming, and he imagined a powerful deceiver, the "evil demon", who tricks us about everything.

Even if he is deceived, Descartes argued, he must exist in order to be deceived. From this comes the cogito, usually summarised as "I think, therefore I am". Descartes then tried to build up knowledge, arguing that God exists and is not a deceiver, so that what we perceive clearly and distinctly is reliable. He also argued for dualism: mind (thinking, unextended) and body (extended in space) are distinct substances.

Descartes is a rationalist: he gave reason a leading role in knowledge, and thought some ideas are innate. Critics raised problems: the "Cartesian circle" (does his proof of God rely on the clear-and-distinct rule that God is supposed to guarantee?), and the interaction problem: if mind and body are completely different, how do they affect each other? Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia pressed him on this in letters.

example.q: Descartes doubts that he has a body. Why can he not doubt that he is thinking?
steps: Doubting is a kind of thinking.
If he doubts, someone must be doubting.
So the thinker exists, at least while thinking.
example.a: Doubt itself shows a thinker exists (the cogito).

analogies.tech: A computer that tests every line of code for errors until it finds something that always works is like Descartes testing beliefs.
analogies.home: Checking whether a shelf is solid by pushing on it from every side before putting books on it.
analogies.sea: A builder drives piles down until they hit bedrock, as Descartes sought a foundation.

stages.mnemonic: Doubt everything, find the one thing doubt cannot touch: the doubter.
terms: Method of doubt
Testing beliefs by trying to doubt them, to find certain foundations.
Cogito
Descartes's claim that his own existence as a thinker cannot be doubted.
Dualism
The view that mind and body are two distinct kinds of thing.
Rationalism
The view that reason, not only the senses, is a major source of knowledge.

misc.wrong: Descartes thought we should doubt everything forever.
misc.right: Doubt was a method to reach certainty, not a permanent attitude. He held that we can have secure knowledge.

stages.limits: Interpreters disagree on whether the cogito is an inference or an immediate insight, and on how his proofs of God work.

trip.prompt: Find the "evil demon" and the cogito in the article.

questions.q: What was the purpose of Descartes's method of doubt?
o: To find beliefs that cannot be doubted
To prove that nothing can ever be known
To show that the senses are always reliable
To replace reason with faith
questions.why: He aimed for certain foundations.

questions.q: What does the cogito claim?
o: The doubting thinker must exist
Only physical matter exists in the world
God is a deceiver who rules our thoughts
All ideas come only from sense experience
questions.why: Even deception requires someone deceived.

questions.q: The evil demon argument is meant to show...
o: Even beliefs that seem obvious could be doubted
Evil demons are real and control the world
The senses never mislead anyone
Dreams are always more real than waking life
questions.why: It extends doubt as far as possible.

questions.q: Dualism says...
o: Mind and body are distinct kinds of thing
Everything that exists is purely material
Everything that exists is purely mental
Neither mind nor body really exists
questions.why: It is substance dualism.

questions.q: Which problem did Princess Elisabeth press?
o: How can mind and body interact?
How could God be present everywhere at once?
Why do dreams seem so real to us?
Who first discovered the rules of mathematics?
questions.why: The interaction problem.

questions.q: Rationalists give reason an important role. Which claim fits this?
o: Some knowledge, like maths, can be gained by reason alone
All knowledge, including mathematics, comes only from sense experience
Knowledge of anything at all is impossible
Only the testimony of authorities gives knowledge
questions.why: Rationalism contrasts with strict empiricism.

questions.q: Why is the Cartesian circle a worry?
o: He seems to use clear and distinct perception to prove God, and God to guarantee it
It shows that his chain of doubt can never come to an end or stop
He gave no argument for God at all
He doubted every thought including his own existence
questions.why: The reasoning risks assuming what it needs to prove.

questions.q: Match each term with its meaning.
pairs: Mind and body are different substances
questions.why: These are core terms.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why Descartes thinks "I am deceived" shows "I exist".
questions.model: To be deceived or to doubt requires someone who is deceived or doubting. So the thinker must exist, at least while thinking.
questions.why: The inference is the heart of the cogito.

questions.q: A critic says "There are thoughts, but that does not show there is an I." What is this?
o: An objection to the step from thinking to a self
A proof that dualism is true and that the self is a separate substance
An agreement with Descartes' reasoning
A claim that thoughts need a body
questions.why: Some thinkers, such as Hume and Lichtenberg, questioned the self.

panel.q: Is it fair to say Descartes was a sceptic?
o: He used doubt to defeat scepticism
No, he believed that nothing can be known
No, he denied that reason can find truth
Yes, he rejected mathematics and the senses for good
panel.why: He used doubt as a tool.

panel.q: Describe one strength and one weakness of dualism.
panel.model: Strength: it fits the sense that conscious experience is different from physical stuff. Weakness: it is hard to explain how a non-physical mind causes changes in a physical body.
panel.why: Both points are standard in the debate.

panel.q: Why can a dream be a problem for knowing the world through the senses?
o: Dreams can feel just like waking, so feeling alone does not prove reality
Dreams are always vague and easy to spot
Dreams are always true accounts of reality
Dreams only occur in people who have been studying the world too closely
panel.why: Descartes uses dreaming to raise doubt.

teach.model: Descartes doubted everything to find a firm foundation. He found the cogito: the doubter exists. He argued that mind and body are distinct and that reason is a key source of knowledge. For example, an evil demon scenario.

stages.title: John Locke and empiricism
stages.hook: Is a newborn baby's mind like a blank page, or does it start with built-in ideas? What evidence could decide?
explain: John Locke (1632 to 1704), an English philosopher, argued in An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689) that all our ideas come from experience: from sensation (senses) and reflection (noticing our own mental activity). He compared the mind at birth to a blank slate, often called "tabula rasa". This is empiricism, the view that knowledge comes mainly from experience.

Locke distinguished primary qualities (like shape and motion, in objects themselves) from secondary qualities (like colour and taste, which depend on how objects affect perceivers). He also discussed personal identity, suggesting it depends on continuity of consciousness and memory. Critics asked about gaps in memory and about whether the account is circular.

In political thought, Locke's Two Treatises of Government argued that people have natural rights to life, liberty and property, that governments are created by consent to protect these, and that people may resist a government that breaks the trust. His Letter Concerning Toleration argued for religious toleration (with limits). His ideas influenced later constitutions. Scholars also criticise Locke's links to colonial ventures and slavery-related investments, and discuss how this fits with his writing on liberty.

example.q: Someone born blind has never seen red. According to Locke, can they have a full idea of red?
steps: Locke says ideas arise from experience.
Without sight there is no sensation of red.
So they would lack that idea, though they could learn facts about it.
example.a: They lack the sensation-based idea of red.

analogies.home: A child who has never tasted a lemon cannot know its taste from description alone.
analogies.city: A town builds its map by surveying streets, not by guessing; ideas come from experience.
analogies.nature: A seed grows according to soil and weather; Locke compared minds shaped by experience.

stages.mnemonic: Locke: Look, Listen, Learn; the mind starts as a slate, then writes.
terms: Empiricism
The view that knowledge comes mainly from experience.
Tabula rasa
Latin for "blank slate", used for Locke's view that the mind starts without innate ideas.
Primary qualities
Features such as shape and motion, in objects themselves.
Consent
Agreement by those governed that gives a government its authority.

misc.wrong: Locke claimed people know nothing before experience.
misc.right: Locke denied innate ideas, but he thought the mind has abilities to compare and reason with the ideas that experience provides.

stages.limits: Scholars debate Locke's views of personal identity, and criticise his involvement with colonial ventures and the tension with his ideas on liberty.

trip.prompt: Find his arguments about natural rights and consent.

questions.q: What are the two sources of ideas in Locke's Essay?
o: Sensation and reflection
Faith and fear
Dreams and angels
Authority and tradition
questions.why: Experience comes through senses and inner reflection.

questions.q: Which term describes Locke's epistemology?
o: Empiricism
Rationalism
Stoicism
Idealism
questions.why: He stressed experience.

questions.q: Which are primary qualities?
o: Shape and motion
Colour and taste
Smell and sound
Beauty and sadness
questions.why: Primary qualities belong to objects themselves.

questions.q: Locke's political view of government says authority comes from...
o: The consent of the governed
Divine right, passed down to kings
Inheritance from earlier rulers alone
Force and the strength of armies
questions.why: Governments are made to protect rights.

questions.q: What natural rights did Locke emphasise?
o: Life, liberty and property
Fame, power and high rank
Silence and rest from labour
Wealth, luxury and leisure
questions.why: These are his classic trio.

questions.q: Locke suggests personal identity depends on...
o: Continuity of consciousness
Having the same body only
Having the same name
Having the same job
questions.why: Memory and consciousness link past and present.

questions.q: An objection to Locke's memory view: an old man remembers being a boy, the boy remembered a baby moment, but the old man forgot being a baby. What is the issue?
o: Identity may not be transitive if it depends on direct memory
There is no problem with the account, since memory always links all stages
Boys have no memory of their childhood
Old men cannot remember anything
questions.why: It is the "brave officer" objection raised by Thomas Reid.

questions.q: Match each idea to Locke.
questions.why: These are Locke's ideas.

questions.q: Why would Locke reject the idea that everyone is born knowing basic moral truths?
questions.model: He argued that if such truths were innate, everyone, including children, would know them, but they do not, so ideas come from experience.
questions.why: Locke gave this kind of argument against innate ideas.

questions.q: A government breaks its trust and harms the people. Which Lockean view follows?
o: People may resist or replace it
They must obey in every case
They should leave the world
Nothing can be done
questions.why: Consent can be withdrawn when trust is broken.

panel.q: A critic says Locke's rights talk sits uneasily with his colonial activity. How should we describe this?
o: A real tension that scholars discuss
No tension exists
Locke was never in contact with colonies
It is only a rumour
panel.why: Locke helped draft a Carolina constitution and held investments.

panel.q: How does empiricism differ from rationalism?
panel.model: Empiricists say knowledge comes mainly from sense experience, while rationalists give more weight to reason and possibly innate ideas.
panel.why: This is a broad contrast.

panel.q: Why did Locke's ideas about consent influence later constitutions?
o: They justified limited government based on the people
They endorsed rule by absolute monarchs who answer to no one at all
They denied that people have rights
They argued that laws should be abolished
panel.why: His ideas fed into later political thought.

teach.model: Locke said ideas come from experience, through the senses and reflection. The mind starts like a blank slate. In politics, governments exist by consent to protect rights like life, liberty and property. For example, a blind person lacks the idea of colour.

points.ask: What is the mind at birth?

stages.title: David Hume and scepticism
stages.hook: The sun has risen every day of your life. Does that prove it will rise tomorrow? What kind of reason could prove it?
explain: David Hume (1711 to 1776), a Scottish philosopher, developed empiricism with great rigour. In A Treatise of Human Nature and An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding he divided our perceptions into impressions (vivid, direct experiences) and ideas (fainter copies). He argued that every idea ultimately derives from impressions.

Hume raised the problem of induction. We believe the future will be like the past, for example that the sun will rise. But we cannot prove it by logic (the opposite is not contradictory), and using past experience to show the future will resemble the past would assume what is to be proved. He suggested that such beliefs are driven by habit or custom, not by deductive proof. On causation, he argued that we observe events following each other (constant conjunction) but never see a necessary link.

Hume also questioned a fixed self (we find only a bundle of perceptions) and argued that reason alone cannot tell us what we ought to do, the "is-ought" problem: from facts about what is, we cannot simply deduce what ought to be without a further moral premise. He thought moral judgements rest on sentiment. Philosophers disagree on whether Hume was a sceptic, a naturalist or both. Hume also wrote racist remarks that modern scholars criticise.

example.q: Every swan you have seen is white. Does that prove all swans are white?
steps: Past observations show a pattern.
They do not logically guarantee the next case.
So the conclusion is only probable. Black swans exist in Australia.
example.a: No, induction gives probability, not proof.

analogies.farm: A farmer expects the rain to follow dark clouds because it usually has, not because of a proven law.
analogies.tech: A model trained on past data predicts future data on the assumption that the future resembles the past.
analogies.sport: A coach expects a star player to score again based on past games, which is reasonable but not guaranteed.

stages.mnemonic: Hume: habit makes us expect; logic cannot prove it.
terms: Impression
A vivid direct experience, in Hume's terms.
Induction
Reasoning from observed cases to unobserved ones.
Constant conjunction
Events repeatedly found together, which Hume says is all we observe in causation.
Is-ought gap
The point that facts alone do not logically yield values.

misc.wrong: Hume proved that the sun might not rise, so science is useless.
misc.right: Hume pointed out that induction cannot be proved by logic. He did not recommend abandoning it; he said it is how human beings naturally reason.

stages.limits: Interpreters disagree on Hume's views of causation (sceptical or realist) and on how he treated moral judgement. His racist remarks are criticised.

trip.prompt: Find the problem of induction and the is-ought problem.

questions.q: Hume's problem of induction concerns...
o: Justifying belief that the future resembles the past
Proving by pure logic alone that God must exist in the world
Counting how many numbers there are
Defining what makes something beautiful
questions.why: We cannot prove it by logic or by experience without circularity.

questions.q: What did Hume say we observe in causation?
o: One event followed by another
A necessary link between the cause and effect
A hidden force that pushes things along
A moral duty on every event
questions.why: We see sequence, not necessity.

questions.q: According to Hume, belief that the sun will rise is mainly driven by...
o: Habit or custom
Logical proof
Authority
Magic
questions.why: It is natural, not demonstrated.

questions.q: The is-ought gap says...
o: Facts alone do not logically entail values
Ought can always be deduced from what is
What is can never be known at all
Moral claims are facts of physics
questions.why: We need a further normative premise.

questions.q: Hume on the self:
o: He found only a bundle of perceptions
He found a permanent soul at its centre
He found the body to be the self
He found a clock that kept time for him
questions.why: He questioned a simple unchanging self.

questions.q: A scientist says "Every sample so far behaved this way, so the next will too." Which is the Humean point?
o: This is an inductive step with no logical proof
It is a deduction from a general law
It is circular but proves the point
It is false because science cannot be trusted
questions.why: Induction is the type of reasoning at stake.

questions.q: Match each term with its example.
pairs: Facts do not alone say what we must do
questions.why: Hume's terms.

questions.q: A friend says: "Science rests on induction, which Hume refuted, so science is irrational." What is the best reply?
o: Hume showed induction lacks a deductive proof, not that it is unreasonable to use
Hume proved that science is false, so we should abandon all of it
Hume rejected all reasoning from experience
Hume showed that induction is a form of deduction
questions.why: Responses include probability, pragmatic and Popperian replies.

questions.q: Why can we not justify induction by pointing out that it has worked in the past?
questions.model: That argument uses induction to defend induction: it assumes the future will resemble the past in order to show that it will, which is circular.
questions.why: This is the core of Hume's argument.

questions.q: Which of these is a "black swan" lesson?
o: One counterexample can overturn a generalisation
Swans are always black, so colour is a reliable guide in biology
All swans are white without exception
Birds do not belong in logic
questions.why: Generalisations from limited observation can fail.

panel.q: Karl Popper responded to induction by...
o: Saying science proceeds by conjecture and attempted refutation
Saying induction is perfectly certain and needs no further defence
Rejecting science as unreliable
Denying that observation matters
panel.why: Popper emphasised falsification.

panel.q: Explain why the is-ought gap matters for arguments in ethics.
panel.model: Moral conclusions cannot be derived from purely factual premises; an argument needs an additional moral premise, so we must examine and defend those premises explicitly.
panel.why: Philosophers debate whether the gap can be bridged.

panel.q: A critic notes that Hume still used reasoning in his own life. How does this relate to his view?
o: He said nature leads us to reason and believe despite lack of proof
He gave up reasoning in daily life and lived only by instinct
He lived alone and avoided others
He claimed to have proved induction
panel.why: He said habit makes us believe.

teach.model: Hume said all ideas come from impressions. He raised the problem of induction: we cannot logically prove the future will resemble the past. We believe it by habit. He also pointed out the is-ought gap. For example, the sun rising.

points.ask: What is the problem of induction?

stages.title: Immanuel Kant and critical philosophy
stages.hook: A shopkeeper never cheats customers because cheating hurts business. A second shopkeeper never cheats because it is wrong. Do they differ morally, and how?
explain: Immanuel Kant (1724 to 1804), who lived in Königsberg in Prussia, tried to combine rationalism and empiricism. In the Critique of Pure Reason (1781) he argued that experience requires the mind to organise what it receives using forms such as space and time and categories such as cause. We know things as they appear to us (phenomena), not as they are in themselves (noumena).

In ethics Kant held that morality is based on reason and duty, not on consequences or desire. A good will acts from duty. The categorical imperative is a command that binds without exceptions based on our wishes. One formulation says: act only on principles you could will to be universal laws. Another says: treat humanity, in yourself and others, never merely as a means but always also as an end. Because rational beings can give themselves moral law, they have autonomy and dignity.

Example: lying promises. If everyone made false promises when convenient, promising would collapse, so the principle cannot be universalised. Critics ask what happens when duties conflict (such as honesty versus protecting a friend), whether motives matter more than outcomes, and whether Kant's formulations give clear answers. Kant also held views on race that are rejected today; scholars discuss how that affects reading his universal claims.

example.q: Can you will a world where everyone breaks promises when it suits them?
steps: Imagine the principle becoming a universal law.
Promising would lose meaning.
So the principle fails the test.
example.a: No: the principle cannot be universalised.

analogies.city: Traffic works because everyone follows the same rules; Kant asks if your rule could work for all.
analogies.sport: A game needs everyone to follow the rules; a cheater depends on others obeying them.
analogies.home: A family that expects honesty from everyone cannot also make exceptions for itself without losing trust.

stages.mnemonic: Kant: Could everyone do it? Would it use someone as a mere tool?
terms: Categorical imperative
A moral requirement that applies regardless of wishes.
Autonomy
Self-rule by reason; giving oneself the moral law.
Good will
Acting from duty, the only thing Kant called good without qualification.
Phenomena and noumena
Things as they appear to us versus as they are in themselves.

misc.wrong: Kant said we should follow any rule without thinking.
misc.right: Kant required that principles be tested by reason and respect for persons, not blind obedience.

stages.limits: Kant's examples (such as never lying) are debated, as are his racist views and how to apply the formulations when duties conflict.

trip.prompt: Find the formulations of the categorical imperative.

questions.q: What does Kant say makes an action morally good?
o: Acting from duty and a good will
Producing the most pleasure for the most people
Fitting the customs of one's society
Being popular with one's neighbours
questions.why: Moral worth lies in motive of duty.

questions.q: The universalisation test asks...
o: Could everyone adopt this principle?
Would this principle benefit me personally?
Is the act allowed by the law?
Is the act popular with most people?
questions.why: It tests consistency.

questions.q: The humanity formula says treat people...
o: Never merely as a means, but also as ends
Only as tools for one's own purposes
Only as strangers to be avoided
Only as customers in a market
questions.why: Respect for persons.

questions.q: Autonomy for Kant means...
o: Self-governance by reason
Doing whatever you like
Obeying a king
Avoiding all rules
questions.why: We give ourselves the moral law.

questions.q: Which promise fails the universalisation test?
o: Make a false promise to get money
Keep a promise even when it is hard
Tell the truth when asked
Help a friend who is in need
questions.why: Universal false promising would destroy promising.

questions.q: Phenomena are...
o: Things as they appear to us
Things as they are in themselves
The gods of the Greek tradition
The numbers used in mathematics
questions.why: Noumena are things in themselves.

questions.q: A critic poses: "A murderer asks where your friend is hiding. Must you tell the truth?" This tests...
o: Whether duties can conflict with exceptionless rules
Whether Kant liked to listen to music while he was writing
Whether murderers really exist
Whether dreams can be known
questions.why: Kant himself discussed it and many disagree with his reply.

questions.q: Match each idea to its meaning.
pairs: Ruled by outside desires or authority
questions.why: Kantian terms.

questions.q: Explain why Kant says a shopkeeper who is honest only to keep customers does not show full moral worth.
questions.model: The act is correct but the motive is self-interest, so it has no moral worth in Kant's view; moral worth requires acting from duty.
questions.why: Critics argue this view is too strict.

questions.q: Which is a common criticism of Kantian ethics?
o: It can be rigid when duties conflict
It ignores reason altogether
It judges acts only by pleasure
It has no principles at all
questions.why: Rigidity and conflicts are standard objections.

panel.q: Is the universalisation test about the actual results of everyone acting?
o: It asks whether the principle is consistent as a universal law
Yes, it is only about the outcomes of the act when all do it
No, it is only about the emotions felt
It is about what the law courts decide
panel.why: The test is about whether the maxim can be universally willed without contradiction.

panel.q: Contrast Kant's approach with a purely consequence-based approach.
panel.model: Kant bases rightness on duty and respect for persons, whatever the results, while consequence-based views judge actions by their outcomes.
panel.why: The two approaches can give different answers.

panel.q: Why does Kant link dignity to autonomy?
o: Rational beings can give themselves moral law
Dignity comes from wealth and rank
Dignity is inherited from one's family
Dignity is a feeling of pride
panel.why: Autonomy grounds respect for persons.

teach.model: Kant said the mind shapes experience and that morality is based on duty and reason. The categorical imperative asks if a principle could be universal and whether people are treated as ends. For example, false promises fail.

stages.title: Jean-Jacques Rousseau and political philosophy
stages.hook: Imagine living with no government or laws at all. Would people be mostly peaceful or in conflict? Why do thinkers disagree?
explain: Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712 to 1778), born in Geneva, wrote Discourse on Inequality (1755) and The Social Contract (1762). He asked what a legitimate society looks like. The Social Contract opens by noting that humans are born free yet are everywhere in chains.

Rousseau imagined a "state of nature" as a thought experiment, not necessarily a historical fact. He argued that humans have a natural self-love (amour de soi) and compassion, and that social life creates comparison and vanity (amour-propre), leading to inequality. He thought legitimate authority comes from a social contract in which people join together and obey the general will, the common good that citizens as a whole will, not just the sum of private interests.

Critics argued that the general will could justify pressure on individuals (Rousseau wrote that someone who refuses it may be "forced to be free"), and that Rousseau's views on women's roles were limited. Supporters highlight his demand for equality and participation. Rousseau also wrote Emile on education, urging respect for a child's development. He is often compared and contrasted with Hobbes (who thought life without government would be a war of all against all) and Locke.

example.q: A town votes on whether to keep a shared well clean. How might Rousseau frame the vote?
steps: Ask what serves the common good.
Not merely what each wants alone.
The general will aims at the common good.
example.a: The general will looks to the common good.

analogies.city: A park is for everyone; its rules express shared interests.
analogies.farm: Villagers share irrigation; each depends on the others to keep channels open.
analogies.home: A household rule is more likely followed if members helped make it.

stages.mnemonic: Free by nature, bound by contract, guided by the general will.
terms: State of nature
A hypothetical condition without government used to reason about politics.
Social contract
An agreement, real or hypothetical, that justifies political authority.
General will
The will of the people as a whole aimed at the common good.
Amour-propre
A self-regard based on comparison with others.

misc.wrong: Rousseau said return to nature and abandon society.
misc.right: Rousseau did not recommend returning to a primitive life; he asked how a just society can combine freedom and common rules.

stages.limits: Rousseau's general will is interpreted very differently, and his remarks about women are criticised.

trip.prompt: Find how Rousseau's state of nature differs from Hobbes's.

questions.q: Rousseau's Social Contract asks...
o: How can authority be legitimate?
How can a state win wars against rivals?
How can merchants trade goods most fairly?
How can people travel safely between cities?
questions.why: It is about legitimacy.

questions.q: What is the general will?
o: The common good willed by citizens as a whole
Whatever a majority happens to want
The wish of the ruler of the state
A secret plan made by a small group of powerful citizens
questions.why: It aims at the common interest.

questions.q: Rousseau thought inequality grew with...
o: Comparison and property in society
Climate and geography alone
Being alone in nature
The growth of music and art
questions.why: Social comparison drives amour-propre.

questions.q: Which thinker described a war of all against all?
o: Hobbes
Rousseau
Locke
Kant
questions.why: Hobbes described this condition.

questions.q: Is Rousseau's state of nature a historical claim?
o: It is a thought experiment
It is a documented history
It is a maths proof
It is a legal case
questions.why: He said it may never have existed.

questions.q: A critic says the general will could silence minorities. This is...
o: A common worry about majority-based or collective notions
A strong praise for the idea of the general will as a safeguard
A joke made by his critics
A proof that the idea is perfect
questions.why: Interpreters debate it.

questions.q: Match thinker with view.
pairs: Strong ruler needed to avoid conflict
questions.why: Social contract thinkers differ.

questions.q: Rousseau's Emile argued that education should...
o: Respect a child's development
Punish children to teach them to obey
Avoid learning until they are adults
Prepare children for soldiering
questions.why: He emphasised natural stages of development.

questions.q: How does Rousseau's idea of the general will differ from simply adding up what each person wants?
questions.model: The general will aims at the common good that citizens share, while the sum of private wants might reflect selfish interests that conflict with it.
questions.why: Interpretation of the difference is debated.

questions.q: Why might Rousseau support direct participation in lawmaking?
o: Citizens should obey laws they have helped make
Kings are always wiser than citizens, so citizens should not rule
Voting is of no use to anyone
Law needs no consent from people
questions.why: Obeying self-made laws is freedom.

panel.q: Which statement best compares Hobbes and Rousseau?
o: Hobbes saw conflict without government while Rousseau saw society as corrupting natural goodness
Both saw natural life as peaceful and gentle until states appeared
Both agreed on everything about human nature
Neither of them wrote about politics
panel.why: Their pictures of human nature differ, with caveats.

panel.q: Explain why Rousseau wrote that people are "born free and everywhere in chains".
panel.model: He meant that humans are naturally free but social institutions and inequality bind them, so he asked how law could be made legitimate and free.
panel.why: The line opens The Social Contract.

panel.q: Why do some thinkers warn that "forced to be free" can be dangerous?
o: It can justify coercion in the name of the general good
It praises liberty and is free from all risk of misuse by rulers
It is a joke made by Rousseau
It is a phrase taken from Kant
panel.why: Critics worry about abuse of authority.

teach.model: Rousseau asked how a society can be legitimate. He proposed a social contract where citizens obey the general will aimed at the common good. He thought social comparison creates inequality. For example, a town deciding about a shared well.

stages.title: Arthur Schopenhauer and the philosophy of will
stages.hook: Why do desires seem never to end: when we get one thing, a new want appears? Is that a fact about us, and what could we do about it?
explain: Arthur Schopenhauer (1788 to 1860), a German philosopher, published The World as Will and Representation in 1818. He used Kant's idea that we know the world as appearance (representation), and argued that the inner nature of reality, which we can sense in ourselves, is Will: a blind, endless striving. We experience it as desires, hunger and drives.

Because will strives without final satisfaction, Schopenhauer said life swings between suffering from wanting and boredom when wants are satisfied. This makes his outlook pessimistic. He thought temporary relief comes from contemplating art, especially music, which lets us step out of desire. In ethics he argued that compassion (Mitleid) is the basis of morality, because it recognises that others suffer as we do. He admired ideas from the Upanishads and Buddhism and recommended denying the will through ascetic restraint.

Critics ask whether a single metaphysical Will explains all things, whether his pessimism is a fact or a mood, and whether his view fits his life. His thought influenced Nietzsche, Wagner, Freud, Wittgenstein and many writers. Some readers find consolation, not despair, in his emphasis on compassion and aesthetic calm. Scholars also discuss his comments on women and other groups, which are widely criticised.

example.q: You finally buy the thing you wanted for months and feel pleased for a short time, then want another. How does Schopenhauer describe this?
steps: Wanting is a lack that causes suffering.
Satisfaction is brief.
Then boredom or a new want appears.
example.a: A cycle of wanting, brief satisfaction and new wanting.

analogies.music: Listening to music can make us forget our wants for a moment, which Schopenhauer valued.
analogies.nature: A river keeps flowing, unstoppable; he saw will as a blind force like that.
analogies.city: A busy market is full of striving and wanting, with people always after the next thing.

stages.mnemonic: Will wants, wants, wants; art and compassion give rest.
terms: Will
In Schopenhauer, the blind striving at the core of reality and of our desires.
Representation
The world as it appears to us.
Pessimism
The view that suffering outweighs satisfaction in life.
Compassion
Feeling with another person's suffering; for Schopenhauer, the root of morality.

misc.wrong: Schopenhauer said life is meaningless so do nothing.
misc.right: He argued for compassion, aesthetic contemplation and restraint of desire as responses to suffering.

stages.limits: Scholars disagree on whether the Will is a metaphysical claim or a metaphor, and criticise some of his views about women.

trip.prompt: Find the role of music and compassion in his philosophy.

sources: The World as Will and Representation

questions.q: What does Schopenhauer call the inner nature of reality?
o: Will
Reason
Spirit of history
Atoms
questions.why: He claimed the world in itself is Will.

questions.q: According to Schopenhauer, life swings between...
o: Suffering and boredom
Joy and fear
Work and play
Wealth and poverty
questions.why: Wanting causes suffering; satisfaction brings boredom.

questions.q: Which does he say gives temporary relief?
o: Aesthetic contemplation, especially music
Winning prizes, public honours and the praise of others
Gaining wealth and property
Becoming famous and admired
questions.why: Art lets us escape from desire.

questions.q: Schopenhauer based morality on...
o: Compassion
Honour and reputation
Profit and trade
Law and custom
questions.why: He saw compassion as moral foundation.

questions.q: Which traditions did he draw on?
o: Indian philosophy such as the Upanishads and Buddhism
The Stoic school of ancient Greece and Rome alone
African oral traditions alone
Medieval scholasticism alone
questions.why: He knew translations of Indian texts.

questions.q: A person says: "I will be happy once I win this contest." A Schopenhauerian reply:
o: Satisfaction is brief and new wants arise
Winning gives permanent peace of mind
Contests are evil and should be avoided
Happiness cannot be put into words
questions.why: Desire renews.

questions.q: Match concept to meaning.
questions.why: Key terms.

questions.q: Which is a fair critical question?
o: Is the Will a literal claim or a metaphor?
How many sheep did he own?
Who was the tallest person he knew?
What time did he have lunch?
questions.why: Interpretation is debated.

questions.q: Why does Schopenhauer say compassion is the basis of ethics?
questions.model: He holds that compassion recognises that others suffer as we do, which breaks down the sense of being completely separate, and so motivates unselfish action.
questions.why: Critics ask whether compassion alone is enough.

questions.q: How could one object that Schopenhauer's pessimism is too one-sided?
o: Many people find lasting joy, meaning and satisfaction
Everyone already agrees with him, so there is nothing to object to
Pleasure is impossible for anyone
Suffering is only an illusion
questions.why: Positive experiences might count more than he allows.

panel.q: How does Schopenhauer differ from Kant on morality?
o: Compassion rather than duty and reason is basic
He agrees with Kant entirely that duty and reason are the base
He rejects thinking about ethics
He praises power as the highest good
panel.why: He criticised Kant's rationalism in ethics.

panel.q: Describe how a person might apply Schopenhauer's advice in daily life.
panel.model: One might reduce craving for endless wants, seek moments of calm through art or nature, and practise compassion for others' suffering.
panel.why: Individuals may judge this advice differently.

panel.q: Why might Schopenhauer be called an influence on later thinkers?
o: Nietzsche and others responded to his ideas of will and suffering
He wrote nothing that was ever published, so no one could be influenced
No one ever read his books
He was a king whose court spread his ideas
panel.why: Nietzsche began as an admirer and later criticised him.

teach.model: Schopenhauer said the inner nature of the world is a blind Will that never fully rests, causing suffering. Art can give temporary relief and compassion is the basis of morality. For example, wanting then getting then wanting more.

stages.title: Friedrich Nietzsche and the critique of morality
stages.hook: Does "good" always mean the same thing? Could some moral values have started as ways for groups to feel strong or safe? Think before reading.
explain: Friedrich Nietzsche (1844 to 1900), a German philosopher and philologist, wrote works such as Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Beyond Good and Evil and On the Genealogy of Morality. He asked where our moral values come from, what purposes they serve, and whether they help or harm life. This approach is called genealogy.

In the Genealogy he contrasts "master morality" (values like strength and nobility) with "slave morality" (values like humility and pity), which he says arose from the resentment (ressentiment) of the powerless. Scholars debate how literally to read this and how he judged each. When he wrote that "God is dead", he was describing that belief in God was losing its hold in European culture and warning that old foundations of value would crumble, leading to nihilism, the sense that nothing matters. He urged people to create new values.

Other ideas include perspectivism (knowledge is always from perspectives), the will to power (a drive to grow and shape), the Übermensch (a figure who creates values), eternal recurrence (a thought experiment: could you embrace living your life again and again?) and amor fati (love of fate). Nietzsche was misused by Nazi propagandists, aided by edits by his sister, but scholars strongly reject this reading; he criticised antisemitism and nationalism. Interpretations of his thought vary widely.

example.q: A tradition tells children to "never boast". How might a genealogical thinker ask about its origin?
steps: Who benefits from this rule?
What problem did it solve?
Does it help people flourish today?
example.a: Ask where the value came from and what it does.

analogies.sport: Rules of a sport reflect what the group values; one can ask what values they favour.
analogies.city: A city's statues show whom a society chose to honour; a genealogist asks why.
analogies.music: Musical taste changes with culture; a perspectivist notes that every listener hears from a position.

stages.mnemonic: Nietzsche asks of every value: where did you come from, and what do you do for life?
terms: Genealogy
Tracing the origin and development of a value or idea to understand its function.
Ressentiment
A hidden resentment that Nietzsche says shapes some moral values.
Nihilism
The view or feeling that nothing has value or meaning.
Perspectivism
The idea that knowledge always comes from particular perspectives.

misc.wrong: Nietzsche said morality is useless and people should be cruel.
misc.right: Nietzsche criticised certain moral outlooks and asked for self-overcoming and new values. Reading him as endorsing cruelty or political violence is widely rejected.

stages.limits: Nietzsche's texts are aphoristic and ironic, and scholars disagree about nearly every major concept; he was misappropriated by the Nazis.

trip.prompt: Find the sections on master and slave morality and on the death of God.

questions.q: What is genealogy in Nietzsche's sense?
o: Tracing the origins and functions of values
Studying the family trees of rulers
Counting how many people hold a value
Measuring the land a value covers
questions.why: It is a method of historical critique.

questions.q: "God is dead" is best read as...
o: A diagnosis that belief in God no longer grounds European culture
A wish that God would die so that people could be free
A report from a scientific laboratory
A legal rule in a courtroom
questions.why: He described a cultural change and its risks.

questions.q: Nihilism is...
o: The sense that values have no basis
A love of order and certainty that holds all values in place
A love of beauty above all
A branch of natural science
questions.why: The collapse of meaning.

questions.q: Perspectivism claims...
o: All knowing is from some perspective
There are no facts at all, only the interpretations people choose
Only gods can know the truth
Mathematics is false
questions.why: Interpretation is debated, but this is the core.

questions.q: The eternal recurrence is best described as...
o: A thought experiment about affirming one's life
A law of physics saying that energy always returns to its source
A holiday celebrated in Germany
A religious vow taken in church
questions.why: Could you will your life repeating?

questions.q: Which claim about Nietzsche and Nazism is accurate?
o: His work was distorted by others, and he criticised antisemitism and nationalism
He founded the Nazi party and wrote its political programme
He supported its policies as a writer
He lived through the 1940s
questions.why: He died in 1900.

questions.q: Match term and meaning.
pairs: A figure who creates new values
questions.why: Key terms.

questions.q: Why does Nietzsche ask what a value does for life?
o: He evaluates values by their effect on human flourishing
He wants strict rules that everyone must follow without question
He loves boredom and stillness
He hates all forms of thought
questions.why: Values are judged by their life-affirming or life-denying effects.

questions.q: Describe one criticism of genealogy as a way to judge moral values.
questions.model: Critics say that showing where a value came from does not by itself show whether it is true or justified (the genetic fallacy); we also need reasons to assess it.
questions.why: Defenders reply that genealogy can undermine claims to authority.

questions.q: How might a critic of Nietzsche respond to his view of pity?
o: Compassion can be a strength that supports the vulnerable
Pity is always harmful to everyone who gives or receives it
Pity does not really exist
Pity causes wars between nations
questions.why: Many thinkers disagree with him on this.

panel.q: Is it fair to say Nietzsche cheered the "death of God"?
o: He saw it as both a danger and a chance to create new values
Yes, he celebrated it as a victory
He ignored the idea completely
He wrote about trains and railways
panel.why: He warned of nihilism but also called for new values, so neither simple celebration nor simple dismay fits.

panel.q: Explain why Nietzsche is hard to interpret.
panel.model: He wrote in aphorisms, irony and metaphor, changed his emphasis, and left ideas unsystematised, so scholars read him in different ways.
panel.why: This is a general scholarly view.

panel.q: Which question best expresses Nietzsche's challenge to moral thinking?
o: What is the value of our values?
Which king should rule the land?
What is two plus two?
Where are the stars in the sky?
panel.why: He called for a revaluation of values.

teach.model: Nietzsche asked where moral values come from and what they do for life. He wrote about master and slave morality, the death of God, nihilism and self-overcoming. Interpretations vary; he was misused by others. For example, asking who benefits from a rule.

points.ask: What did he test values by?

stages.title: John Stuart Mill and utilitarianism
stages.hook: A runaway tram will hit five people unless you divert it to a track with one person. Many feel pulled in two directions. What principle are you using in each?
explain: John Stuart Mill (1806 to 1873) defended utilitarianism, the view that right actions promote happiness and wrong ones the reverse. In Utilitarianism (1863) he held that the aim is the greatest happiness for the greatest number, counting everyone's happiness equally. Jeremy Bentham, who started this tradition, measured pleasure by quantity; Mill added that quality matters: intellectual and moral pleasures are of higher quality than mere bodily ones.

Mill's On Liberty (1859) states the harm principle: power over a person against their will is justified only to prevent harm to others. He defended freedom of speech, arguing that even false opinions help us understand truths. With Harriet Taylor Mill, he argued for women's equality in The Subjection of Women. He also argued that rules of justice and rights are very important because they protect security, which supports happiness.

Objections: Can happiness be measured and compared? Could utilitarianism justify harming an innocent person for the benefit of many? Is it too demanding? Utilitarians reply with ideas such as rule utilitarianism, which judges rules by their overall results, and by noting that violating rights tends to reduce well-being. Contemporary utilitarians such as Peter Singer apply the idea to global poverty and animals.

example.q: A hospital has one doctor and two emergencies. How would a utilitarian approach the choice?
steps: Estimate the benefit of treating each.
Choose the action that produces the most well-being overall.
Consider long-term effects and fairness too.
example.a: Choose what produces the most overall well-being, counting everyone equally.

analogies.city: A council chooses between a library and a car park by asking which helps more people.
analogies.home: A family plans a holiday by weighing everyone's enjoyment, not just one person's.
analogies.farm: A village chooses how to use shared grazing land by weighing benefit to all.

stages.mnemonic: Mill: Count everyone, weigh quality as well as quantity, and guard freedom.
terms: Utilitarianism
The view that the right action produces the greatest overall well-being.
Harm principle
Mill's claim that liberty may be limited only to prevent harm to others.
Higher pleasures
Pleasures of mind and character, ranked by Mill above merely bodily ones.
Rule utilitarianism
Judging actions by whether they follow rules that tend to maximise well-being.

misc.wrong: Utilitarianism means the majority can do anything to a minority.
misc.right: Mill argued for strong protection of rights and liberty, partly because they promote happiness. Whether utilitarianism can adequately protect minorities is a live objection.

stages.limits: Scholars debate whether Mill is an act or rule utilitarian and how his higher-pleasure claim fits his theory. Mill also worked for the East India Company, and scholars discuss his views on empire.

trip.prompt: Find the harm principle and the quality of pleasures argument.

questions.q: What does utilitarianism say is right?
o: Actions that promote overall well-being
Actions that follow tradition
Actions that please the rulers and keep the state stable
Actions that avoid effort
questions.why: Consequences for well-being decide.

questions.q: Mill added to Bentham the idea that...
o: Pleasures differ in quality
Only quantity counts
Pleasure does not matter
Pain is good
questions.why: He ranked higher pleasures.

questions.q: The harm principle says...
o: Liberty may be limited only to prevent harm to others
Liberty may be limited for any reason that the majority dislikes
There should be no liberty at all
Only kings are free to act
questions.why: On Liberty states this.

questions.q: Which book argued for women's equality, with Harriet Taylor Mill's influence?
o: The Subjection of Women
Utilitarianism, published in 1863
The Republic, by Plato
Leviathan, by Hobbes
questions.why: It was published in 1869.

questions.q: A common objection to act utilitarianism is that it might...
o: Justify harming one innocent for the many
Ignore consequences altogether
Forbid every kind of action
Rely only on duty and rules, whatever the consequences may be
questions.why: It raises rights and justice concerns.

questions.q: Rule utilitarianism judges...
o: Rules by their overall effect on well-being
Individuals by their birth
People by their wealth and the property they own in society
Acts by luck alone
questions.why: It tests rules, not each act.

questions.q: Peter Singer applies utilitarian ideas to...
o: Global poverty and animals
Medieval logic and language
Ancient gods and ritual
Rules of poetry
questions.why: He argues for equal consideration of interests.

questions.q: Match thinker or term and idea.
questions.why: Terms and thinkers.

questions.q: A utilitarian faces the claim "It is wrong to punish an innocent person even if it would please a crowd." How might a utilitarian reply?
questions.model: A utilitarian can argue that punishing innocents harms trust and security and lowers overall well-being in the long run, so it is wrong even by utilitarian reasoning. Critics doubt this always works.
questions.why: This is a standard reply with standard objections.

questions.q: Why might Mill defend freedom of speech?
o: Open debate helps people find truth and avoid dead dogma
Speech is always true, so there is no need to examine it
Speech is always harmless
Governments always know best
questions.why: He argued that even wrong opinions can improve understanding.

panel.q: Does Mill claim that all pleasures are equal in value?
o: No, he ranked higher pleasures above lower
Yes, all pleasures are equal in value
He denied that pleasure matters
He only wrote about law and government
panel.why: He argued competent judges prefer higher pleasures.

panel.q: Compare Kant and Mill on whether a lie that benefits many is acceptable.
panel.model: Kant would stress that lying treats people as means and cannot be universalised, while Mill would assess the consequences for overall well-being, so they can reach different verdicts.
panel.why: Both approaches have refinements.

panel.q: Why is measuring happiness a challenge for utilitarians?
o: Wellbeing is hard to compare across persons
Happiness is already a number on every person
No one is ever happy
Numbers are not allowed in ethics
panel.why: Comparison of experiences is difficult.

teach.model: Mill said the right action promotes the most overall happiness, counting everyone equally, and that some pleasures are higher in quality. His harm principle protects liberty. Critics worry about rights of individuals. For example, a council choosing between a library and a car park.

points.ask: What does the harm principle say?

stages.title: Søren Kierkegaard and existential thought
stages.hook: Some choices cannot be made by calculating alone, like choosing a career, a belief or a way of life. How should a person choose when reason does not decide?
explain: Søren Kierkegaard (1813 to 1855), a Danish thinker, wrote many works, often under pseudonyms, including Either/Or, Fear and Trembling, The Concept of Anxiety and The Sickness unto Death. He is often called a founder of existential thought, which emphasises individual existence, choice and responsibility.

He described three "stages" or spheres of existence: the aesthetic (living for enjoyment and variety), the ethical (committing to duties and relationships) and the religious (a relationship to God that goes beyond the ethical). These are not rigid steps, and he used different voices to explore them. In Fear and Trembling, he reflects on the biblical story of Abraham and Isaac, asking what it means to trust God against ordinary moral understanding; interpretations differ widely.

Kierkegaard spoke of anxiety as the dizziness of freedom, and of despair as a failure to be a self. He criticised the idea that one can understand life purely as a system (against Hegel) and emphasised "subjectivity": some truths must be lived and appropriated by the individual. His "leap of faith" is often read as a commitment that goes beyond proof. Secular and religious existentialists have drawn on him, including Sartre and Heidegger, while others criticise his focus on the individual.

example.q: A student must decide between a safe career and an uncertain passion. How might Kierkegaard describe the choice?
steps: No calculation can fully settle it.
The individual must choose and take responsibility.
Anxiety is part of freedom.
example.a: A personal commitment with anxiety, not a formula.

analogies.home: Choosing a life partner involves trust that no list of pros and cons can fully capture.
analogies.music: A musician commits to a lifetime of practice not knowing success.
analogies.city: Moving to a new country is a leap whose outcome cannot be fully known.

stages.mnemonic: Kierkegaard: the individual chooses, leaps, and owns it.
terms: Existentialism
A tradition stressing individual existence, freedom and responsibility.
Leap of faith
A commitment made without complete proof.
Anxiety
In Kierkegaard, the dizziness of freedom before possibilities.
Pseudonym
A made-up name; Kierkegaard used them to present different viewpoints.

misc.wrong: Kierkegaard said faith is irrational nonsense.
misc.right: He said faith is not provable by reason and requires personal commitment. Whether he is irrationalist is debated.

stages.limits: Interpretations vary on Kierkegaard's pseudonyms and on whether Fear and Trembling suspends ethics, and secular readers adapt his ideas without his religious framework.

trip.prompt: Find the three stages of existence and the leap of faith.

questions.q: Which three spheres did Kierkegaard describe?
o: Aesthetic, ethical and religious
Ancient, modern and future
Rich, poor and middle
Past, present and future
questions.why: These are his spheres of existence.

questions.q: Why did he use pseudonyms?
o: To present different viewpoints
To hide from all of his readers
To save money on printing
Because the law required it
questions.why: They let him explore stances.

questions.q: Anxiety in Kierkegaard is linked to...
o: Freedom and possibility
Rain and storms
Hunger and thirst only
Law and order
questions.why: He called it the dizziness of freedom.

questions.q: "Subjectivity" in Kierkegaard emphasises...
o: Truths that must be personally lived
Public opinion and the views held by most people
Pure data and measurement
Mathematics only
questions.why: Some truths are appropriated by individuals.

questions.q: He criticised Hegel for...
o: Trying to explain existence entirely in a system
Ignoring history altogether
Being too short to be taken seriously in public debate
Studying music instead of ideas
questions.why: He stressed the lived individual.

questions.q: Which is a Kierkegaard-style response to a hard personal choice?
o: Choose and take responsibility
Wait for certainty before acting
Let other people decide for you
Avoid all choices
questions.why: Commitment under uncertainty.

questions.q: A person lives only for enjoyment and variety and becomes bored. Which sphere does this suggest?
o: The aesthetic
The religious
The ethical
The legal
questions.why: Kierkegaard criticised the emptiness of pure aesthetic living.

questions.q: Match term with description.
questions.why: Core terms.

questions.q: Why does Kierkegaard think some life choices cannot be settled by a system or calculation?
questions.model: He argued that matters like faith, love and one's way of life require a personal commitment and responsibility that no general system or proof can make for us.
questions.why: Critics ask whether this undervalues reasons.

questions.q: Which later movement drew on Kierkegaard?
o: Existentialism
Atomism
Stoicism
Scholasticism
questions.why: Sartre and others developed existentialism.

panel.q: Is it fair to read Kierkegaard only as a religious writer?
o: No, many secular thinkers adapt his ideas on choice and anxiety
Yes, because no secular thinker has ever read or used his ideas
He wrote no religious works at all
He wrote only about mathematics
panel.why: His influence is broad.

panel.q: What is one criticism of the leap of faith idea?
panel.model: Critics worry that without reasons it is hard to tell good commitments from arbitrary or harmful ones.
panel.why: Defenders say faith can be reasonable though not demonstrable.

panel.q: Why might the story of Abraham and Isaac be read in different ways?
o: Kierkegaard presents it through a pseudonym and leaves tension
It has only one meaning that all readers have always agreed on
It is a recipe for a feast
It is a map of an ancient journey
panel.why: Interpreters disagree on its moral.

teach.model: Kierkegaard stressed the individual who must choose and take responsibility. He described aesthetic, ethical and religious ways of living, anxiety as the dizziness of freedom, and the leap of faith. Interpretations vary. For example, choosing a career without a formula.
